quote: Leichter läßt sich jedoch wahrscheinlich der Beweis verallgemeinern, welchen ich in meinem Collegheft [-fürs-] über die Quadratur des Kreises geführt habe
english: However, the proof which I gave in my lecture notebook on the quadrature of the circle can probably be generalized more easily.
topic: Hilbert notes plans to generalize a proof from his lecture notes on the quadrature of the circle, to study links between his approach and discriminants and Sturm functions via approximations of f/f', and to extend the method to continued-fraction-type expansions of hypergeometric series to prove irrationality of Bessel functions.

triage.modern_statement: This is a plan for a method, not a precisely stated theorem. Hilbert wanted to take the transcendence/irrationality proof for π (and e) that he had given in his lecture notes on squaring the circle, and make it work for more general functions. This proof was presumably the one he published in 1893 in Math. Ann. 43, 'Über die Transcendenz der Zahlen e und π'; the diary note does not confirm the link. In modern terms the aim is to show that the values at nonzero rational or algebraic points of functions beyond exp are irrational or transcendental. The examples he names are hypergeometric series with continued-fraction-type expansions, such as Bessel functions. Today this belongs to the theory of Siegel E-functions: proving the irrationality, transcendence or algebraic independence of values of Bessel functions like J0(α) and J0'(α) for algebraic α ≠ 0.
triage.answered_by: The Bessel-function goal named on the page was achieved by Carl Ludwig Siegel in his 1929 paper. He introduced E-functions to generalize the Hermite–Lindemann–Weierstrass theorems and proved that J0(α) and J0'(α) are algebraically independent for every nonzero algebraic α. That is much stronger than irrationality. His methods were extended by Shidlovskii (the Siegel–Shidlovskii theorem), and later by Nesterenko, André and Beukers (2006). No source shows that this came from Hilbert's own Collegheft proof or from his f/f' and Sturm-function idea.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 1893 simplified proof of the transcendence of e and π appeared in Mathematische Annalen 43, pp. 216–219.
In 1893 Hilbert simplified Lindemann's transcendence proof for π.

Siegel introduced E-functions in 1929 to generalize the Hermite/Lindemann/Weierstrass theorems. For the Bessel function J0 he proved that J0(z) and J0'(z) are algebraically independent at every nonzero algebraic number.
Siegel introduced E-functions in 1929 as a generalization of the exponential and Bessel functions, and proved a result on the Diophantine nature of Bessel function values.
Siegel's methods were developed further by Shidlovskii, Nesterenko and André, and Beukers proved a refinement in 2006.

triage.why: The diary note describes a research plan rather than a specific conjecture: generalizing the proof of π's transcendence so that it gives irrationality for values of Bessel and hypergeometric functions. The concrete target, irrationality (and in fact transcendence and algebraic independence) of Bessel function values at algebraic points, was settled by Siegel in 1929 and extended in the Siegel–Shidlovskii theory. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems, though it is close in spirit to his 7th. The E-function and G-function area is still active (Beukers 2006, Delaygue, Fresán–Jossen). Confidence is medium for three reasons. First, the identification of the Collegheft proof with the 1893 paper is my inference, not something a source confirms. Second, the f/f'-approximation, discriminant and Sturm-function part of the plan does not match any later result I could find. Third, the search did not check whether Hilbert himself followed up on this.
